thesis: There was no 1990 Grand Cherokee -- the truck took seven years to cross two different car companies (AMC, then Chrysler) before it reached the public in January 1992, and even its most famous moment, driving through a plate-glass window at its own unveiling, is usually misremembered: popular memory puts the company's boss behind the wheel, when it was actually the company's president, with the mayor of Detroit riding along for a stunt built on fake theatrical glass. The real story -- a delayed, disputed, multi-company gestation capped by a stunt more mythologized than accurately recalled -- is more interesting than either the wrong date or the wrong driver.
hook: You've probably heard the story: Jeep's boss drove a brand-new Grand Cherokee through a plate-glass window to launch it. Except it wasn't 1990, it wasn't real glass, and it wasn't the boss driving.
runtime_rationale: Just over 10 minutes -- at the floor of the channel's normal_range_minutes and well below the 12-minute preferred_minutes center. Justification: this episode opens by correcting its own premise (no 1990 car exists), which compresses rather than expands the cold open; several supporting claims are single-sourced background (prod01, prod02, plant01, tech01, gen01) held at medium confidence and used as color rather than expanded into their own beats; one claim (reveal04, Iacocca's role) is unresolved and explicitly excluded from narration; and the price data (price01) is a hedged range rather than a clean number, which shortens rather than pads that beat. Six moderate beats fit comfortably under 12 minutes without stretching thin material.
open_questions: price01: no single canonical 1993 base MSRP was found (figures ranged $18,990-$21,898 across aggregators, possibly reflecting 2-door vs. loaded-4-door confusion). A period Chrysler/Jeep press kit or brochure would resolve this better than aggregator sites.

reveal04: one source claims Iacocca personally delayed the launch to late 1992, but that source (Hagerty Media) returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch and the claim is only known via a search-engine synthesis, not a read source. Worth a retry via an archived/cached version, or a different Chrysler-history source, before deciding whether it belongs in the episode at all.

dev02: the Shinoda design-credit litigation and settlement figure is reputation-sensitive (implies AMC took credit for another designer's work) and currently rests on Wikipedia alone. Worth a second, independent source (a design-history retrospective or period trade-press piece) before leaning on it narratively rather than as a brief aside.

beats.purpose: Open on the famous stunt as commonly (mis)remembered, setting up the corrections that follow.
beats.summary: At its 1992 Detroit debut, a new Jeep was driven up a flight of stairs and through a plate-glass window in front of a stunned crowd -- one of the most talked-about vehicle launches in automotive history, and one popular memory gets wrong in more than one way.
beats.narration_direction: Lead with the spectacle before naming any executive or date specifics -- let the hook's correction land in b2/b4, not here. Do not yet say who was driving.

beats.purpose: Address the episode's own premise head-on: correct the date before building any further narrative on it.
beats.summary: There was no Grand Cherokee in 1990 -- the nameplate simply didn't exist yet. It was still two years from its public debut and wouldn't reach buyers until the 1993 model year.
beats.narration_direction: State this plainly and without apology -- it's a genuine finding, not an error to gloss over. Use it as a pivot into 'so what was happening in 1990?' which leads into b3's development story.

visual_requests.description: The two models the Grand Cherokee was eventually meant to sit between/replace, shown as what actually existed circa 1990.

beats.purpose: Tell the real development story: a project that outlived the company that started it.
beats.summary: The truck's roots go back to roughly 1985, under American Motors -- a company Chrysler didn't even own yet. A 1985 prototype design by stylist Larry Shinoda led to a design-credit dispute that Chrysler later settled for over $200,000, well after buying AMC outright in 1987 and carrying the program forward itself.
beats.narration_direction: This is the beat that answers b2's pivot. Keep dev02 as a brief, clearly-attributed aside ('according to one account') given it's single-sourced and reputation-sensitive -- don't build a whole dramatic sequence on the lawsuit alone.

visual_requests.subject: AMC Kenosha or Chrysler Highland Park facilities, mid-1980s
visual_requests.description: Period-appropriate AMC/Chrysler corporate or design-studio imagery for the development-era section.

beats.purpose: Deliver the thesis's second correction: who was actually driving, and what was actually real.
beats.summary: The driver through the window wasn't Chrysler's chairman -- that was still Lee Iacocca. It was Bob Lutz, Chrysler's president, who drove from the Jefferson North Assembly Plant with Detroit's mayor riding along and a police escort. The glass itself was fake theatrical 'sugar glass,' built to shatter safely for the cameras.
beats.narration_direction: This is the core corrective beat -- state plainly that popular retellings often get the driver's role wrong, then give the accurate version. Do NOT mention Iacocca ordering a delay (reveal04) -- that claim is unresolved and excluded from narration; if Iacocca is mentioned at all here, it is only to clarify he was chairman and was NOT in the vehicle.

beats.purpose: Ground the spectacle in what a buyer actually got in 1993.
beats.summary: Engines ranged from a 190-horsepower inline-six up to a 245-horsepower V8 by the final model year, plus a diesel sold only outside the US. It launched with a standard driver's airbag on every model and was marketed as the first mid-size SUV offering V8 power -- at a price that, depending on trim and source, ran roughly $19,000 to $22,000.
beats.narration_direction: Use price01's hedged range explicitly -- 'roughly $19,000 to $22,000 depending on trim,' never a single unqualified figure. tech01's 'firsts' language must stay scoped to 'mid-size SUV,' not broadened to 'first SUV ever.'

visual_requests.description: Interior shot and/or V8 engine bay shot for the spec rundown.

beats.purpose: Close on scale: how big this actually got, worldwide.
beats.summary: Jeep built over 1.25 million of them across six model years -- including a rare, one-year-only Grand Wagoneer flagship trim of just 6,378 units -- and assembled them not just in Detroit but in Austria, Argentina, and Venezuela, all while the smaller Cherokee it was meant to eventually succeed kept selling right alongside it.
beats.narration_direction: These are the pack's most straightforward background stats -- state them plainly as the closing 'how big did this actually get' beat. All four are single-sourced background facts at medium confidence; fine to state directly per their safe_wording, just don't stack extra certainty onto them.
